title: PCA in Practice with Scikit‑Learn 🐍
description: Apply PCA step‑by‑step, choose the right number of components, and interpret explained variance ratios.

slides.title: PCA Workflow 🔄
slides.content:
# Steps to Apply PCA

1. **Scale the data** (StandardScaler). PCA is sensitive to variances.
2. **Instantiate PCA** with `n_components` (number or desired explained variance ratio).
3. **Fit** on training data, then **transform** both train and test.
4. Optionally, inspect `explained_variance_ratio_` and cumulative sum.
5. Use transformed data for downstream models.

PCA also has `inverse_transform` to reconstruct original (approximate) data.

slides.title: Basic PCA Example 🐍
slides.content: Reduce iris (4 features) to 2 components and plot:
slides.codeSnippet:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print("Explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
plt.scatter(X_pca[:,0], X_pca[:,1], c=y)
plt.show()

quizData.question: Why must we scale data before PCA?

options.text: To ensure features with larger variance don’t dominate the principal components
PCA automatically centers but not scales

quizData.explanation: PCA seeks directions of maximum variance; if one feature has much larger numeric range, it will dominate the first PC.

slides.title: Determining n_components Automatically 🤖
slides.content:
# Using Explained Variance Threshold

Instead of specifying k, you can pass a float between 0 and 1:
```
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)  # keep enough components to retain 95% variance
pca.fit(X_scaled)
print(pca.n_components_)  # actual number chosen
```

This is extremely useful when you have hundreds of features and want to compress data while preserving most information.

slides.title: Auto Choose k 🐍
slides.content: Compress digits dataset (64 dim) while keeping 90% variance:
slides.codeSnippet:
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

digits = load_digits()
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(digits.data)

pca = PCA(n_components=0.90)
X_reduced = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print(f"Reduced from {X_scaled.shape[1]} to {pca.n_components_} components")

quizData.question: After applying PCA, you can perfectly reconstruct the original data if you keep all components.
quizData.explanation: True. PCA is an invertible linear transform if you retain all components (no dimension reduction).
